kill_argument: H2, the headline, is a test that the crew's own faithful implementation is expected to fail about one time in three, and the reason is known before any analysis runs. The scikit-learn forest is not randomForest. On 10 of 10 synthetic units it sits $216 (SE $9) below R, through a noisier D forest. That attenuation is proportional to theta, so it should carry over to net_tfa. The 5-fold forest cell alone then falls outside its $287 tolerance with probability 0.24. A failed H2 will therefore mostly re-measure a deviation known before the gate. A passed H2 means no shift above $272-569 was detected, on eight cells checked only at the 2-fold training size. What I attacked that held: the lasso correction. The re-run of check-learner-ports with hdm's zero threshold brings the port to +$0.04 (max $0.36, cor 0.99999997), all four other learners reproduce the first run to the digit, the first run is kept in git (b57c415) and NOTES, and no analysis run exists. I recomputed every port-based p_outside value and the combined 33%, and they match. The forest risk is priced, disclosed and given a reading rule fixed in advance. That is honest, not fatal.

findings.text: The 'not testable' (NT) rule discards rejections as well as passes. hypotheses[1] and design.decision_rules.H2 say an NT cell 'does not count toward H2 either way', and design.tolerance_table marks both lasso cells testable = false. NT is justified by power (the 80%-power detectable shift is $1,072 / $827, more than half the bracketed SE). Power limits what a pass means. It does not weaken a rejection: the per-cell critical value 2.81 is the Bonferroni value for all 10 cells, so counting a lasso rejection keeps the familywise size at or below 5%. As written, a lasso cell $1,500 off still leaves 'H2 holds'. That is the cell most likely to move: no rlasso in scikit-learn, an assumed penalty constant, and off-protocol lasso estimates $788-2,465 from the published cells (sources/notes.md section 5). H3 catches only an upward lasso shift large enough to cross a flexible learner.
findings.evidence: plan.json hypotheses[1]; plan.json design.decision_rules.H2; design.tolerance_table rows plr-lasso-2fold and plr-lasso-5fold (testable: false); sources/notes.md section 5, off-protocol lasso rows
findings.response: Designer: one-sided rule in design.decision_rules.H2 and tolerance_table (counts_as_failure_if_outside true for all 10, counts_as_pass_if_inside false for lasso); size <= 5% over 10 cells; hypotheses[1] wording needs a PI edit.
findings.ruling: hypotheses[1] now says an NT cell outside its tolerance is an H2 failure and inside is not a pass; design.decision_rules.H2 and every tolerance_table row (counts_as_failure_if_outside true for all 10, counts_as_pass_if_inside false for lasso) agree; code/verdict.py h2_holds = n_outside == 0 and all 8 testable inside. The change is disclosed in plan.json disclosures[1].
findings.remedy: Cheaper than any new run: make NT one-sided before any analysis run. An NT cell inside its tolerance is reported as 'not testable at this resolution'. An NT cell outside its tolerance is a detected discrepancy and makes H2 fail. Keep 2.81 for all 10 cells and state the familywise size (at most 5%).

findings.text: Only the lasso port is checked against the authors' software (analysis_plan[0], purpose 'show the lasso is the authors' lasso, not a lookalike'). The four learners that make up all eight testable cells are never compared with rpart, randomForest, gbm or nnet. Yet design.learners lists known deviations for each. nnet: identity instead of logistic output, unpenalized biases, Glorot instead of U(-0.7, 0.7) initialization, and L-BFGS-B stopping after about 88 iterations for Y on an absolute 2.2e-9 loss change against nnet's reltol 1e-8 / maxit 1000. On [0,1]-scaled net_tfa the loss is far below 1, so that is a relative tolerance two to three orders of magnitude looser (runs/timing-synthetic/timing.json: iters_mean_nnet_y 87.8, and restarts add nothing). Tree: a sklearn pruning path and different CV folds. Boosting: friedman_mse and sklearn's exponential-loss leaf values. Any of these can plausibly move a cell by more than its $209-438 tolerance. Under design_constraints[1] a failed cell can then only be 'explained' by a conjecture from the list, and the seed asks the crew to explain differences. The cost of measuring this is low: rpart 4.1.24, randomForest 4.7.1.2, gbm 2.3.1 and nnet 7.3.20 are installed here (I checked package versions only and ran no model).
findings.response: Designer: added pre-gate data-prep run check-learner-ports (design.check_learner_ports, analysis_plan[0], task e-learner-ports): all five ports vs the authors' ML_Functions.R calls on 10 synthetic units, R-seed spread as yardstick, pass rules fixed, failures recorded as measured deviations, never re-tuned.
findings.ruling: check-learner-ports ran (runs/check-learner-ports/run.json, exit 0) with all five ports against the authors' verbatim ML_Functions.R calls (git blob checked), R-seed yardstick and pass rules fixed before the run. Its results raise a new problem, F7.
findings.remedy: Extend step 0 into a data-prep run, check-learner-ports, on the same synthetic Y/D draws built from the real covariates (never net_tfa or e401). For each learner and nuisance, compare held-out predictions from the crew port with those of the R function called exactly as ML_Functions.R calls it. Use the R-versus-R spread across two seeds as the yardstick for the stochastic learners. Optionally also compare theta on a synthetic outcome with a known coefficient. Fix pass thresholds now. Record a failure as a measured deviation, with its size, before any analysis run. Do not re-tune afterwards.

findings.text: check-noctrl leaves an open fork. If the full-sample no-controls estimate misses $19,559, the crew 'stops until the PI decides', with no rule set in advance. data/CODEBOOK.md has already found the obvious alternative: the 9,275-row Abadie income band, which the authors' code says it follows. Choosing the sample after seeing the raw eligibility gap is the fork the track rules forbid.
findings.response: Designer: design.sample_rule: all 9,915 rows only, switching forbidden; the 9,275 Abadie band appears only as a pre-stated descriptive no-controls OLS in check-noctrl; a mismatch is reported and the main runs proceed.
findings.ruling: design.sample_rule fixes all 9,915 rows and forbids switching; the Abadie band is a pre-stated descriptive diagnostic in check-noctrl.
findings.remedy: State now which alternative samples are admissible (for example only the 9,275-row band) and the rule for switching. Any switch is a disclosed deviation, and both samples' main runs are then reported.

findings.text: se_rep assumes the crew's split-to-split SD equals the published one. hypotheses[1] then reads a cell outside its tolerance as 'evidence that software, tuning or learner differences, not split randomness, move the estimate'. A port that is noisier across splits fails more often than 0.5% per cell even when its centre matches, for example nnet with one random start and early stopping. Such a failure is a variance difference, not a location shift. The design has no pre-set wording for this case. Diagnostic 9a is reported, but nothing links it to how a failure is read.
findings.response: Designer: decision_rules.H2_reading_of_failures adds tol_obs from our own split MAD next to every failed cell, with fixed wording (variance difference vs centre shift); never changes the verdict.
findings.ruling: design.decision_rules.H2_reading_of_failures adds tol_obs with fixed wording and never changes the verdict.
findings.remedy: Keep the published-noise tolerance as the only test. Next to each failed cell, pre-specify a descriptive tolerance recomputed with the crew's observed 1.4826 x MAD. If the failure disappears under it, word the result as 'outside tolerance, consistent with higher split noise in the replication'.

findings.text: The track's design rules ask for effect sizes against a meaningful baseline. The design reports dollars and units of the published SE only. No baseline is planned, such as mean net_tfa of ineligible households or the SD of net_tfa.
findings.response: Designer: design.baseline: verdict reports mean net_tfa of ineligible households, SD of net_tfa and each cell as % and SD units.
findings.ruling: design.baseline adds the ineligible mean, eligible mean and SD of net_tfa, descriptive only.
findings.remedy: Add one pre-specified baseline quantity to the verdict run; it is descriptive and changes no test.

findings.text: The port check measured a forest deviation large enough to change what H2 means, and the design was not revised after it (log.jsonl: last design-revised 13:01:45Z, check finished 13:29:47Z). On all 10 synthetic units the Python forest theta lies below R seed A (shift -$216, SE $9; rms_port $218 against rms_seed $16, i.e. 13x, not the '21x' in runs/NOTES.md). The gap sits in the D forest: median out-of-fold RMSE of m_hat 0.4798 (Python) vs 0.4715 (R), cor 0.973 vs 0.995 between R seeds. A noisier cross-fitted m_hat attenuates the partialling-out ratio by roughly E[(m - m_hat)^2]/E[(D - m_hat)^2], a bias proportional to theta itself, so with published forest cells near $9,100-9,250 (synthetic truth 9,000) the shift should carry over to net_tfa roughly unchanged. My arithmetic with the tolerance_table's se_rep and se_pub: at a -$216 shift the K = 5 forest cell (tolerance $287, combined SE $102) falls outside its tolerance with probability about 0.24 (0.19-0.31 for shift +/- 2 SE) and the K = 2 cell ($438, SE $156) about 0.08, against the 0.005 per cell the plan states. hypotheses[1] still says 'a faithful re-implementation fails H2 about 5% of the time' and reads any cell outside its tolerance as evidence that 'software, tuning or learner differences, not split randomness, move the estimate'. design.check_learner_ports.on_failure says only that the measured deviation is the 'first candidate explanation', with no rule for when it does or does not explain a failed cell. So the main headline (H2) will largely re-measure a deviation already known before the gate, and the attribution is left open until after the results. The forest K = 5 cell, where the effect is largest, was not checked (K = 2 only).

findings.response: Designer: tolerance_table now carries each cell's measured port shift and p_outside (forest K=5 0.24, K=2 0.08); decision_rules.H2_size_under_measured_ports and hypotheses[1] state H2's false-failure rate (~33%, ~46% with lasso rescaled); reading rule fixed (same sign and |diff - shift| <= tol, else 'not explained'); K=5 not checked is stated.
findings.ruling: Fixed in plan.json. Every tolerance_table row now carries port_shift_measured, port_shift_se, p_outside_given_shift and its +-2 SE range. I recomputed the forest values from p = P(|N(shift, tol/2.81)| > tol): K=5 0.243 (0.19-0.305), K=2 0.077. I also recomputed the combined H2 false-failure rate, 1 - prod(1 - p) = 0.331. decision_rules.H2_size_under_measured_ports and hypotheses[1] state about 33%. The reading rule (same sign and |diff - shift| <= tol) is fixed in H2_reading_of_failures, and verdict.py writes it. The amendment is disclosed in disclosures[2]. The PI's ruling (a), which keeps the forest port, is recorded. That K = 5 was not checked is stated in every K = 5 row and in threats[12].
findings.remedy: No new run is needed. Before the gate: (a) state in plan.json, per cell, the measured synthetic shift and the H2 failure probability it implies (forest about 0.08 / 0.24; lasso, see F9), and amend the 5% size sentence in hypotheses[1] to say it holds for a port without a measured deviation; (b) fix a reading rule now, for example: a cell outside its tolerance is described as 'consistent with the port deviation measured on synthetic data' only if diff has the sign of shift_L and |diff - shift_L| <= tolerance, and otherwise as 'not explained by the measured port deviation'; a forest pass is reported as a pass despite the measured shift; (c) the PI decides explicitly, before the gate, whether the forest port stays as it is, with the deviation disclosed. Re-implementing the forest to match randomForest is possible only on synthetic evidence and before the gate, with check-learner-ports re-run and both results kept. The narrowing in (a)-(b) is cheaper.

findings.text: The candidate list for the forest (design.candidate_deviations.forest) leaves out the most likely cause of the measured D-forest deviation. design_constraints[1] lets the paper explain a failed cell only with a candidate on that list. runs/NOTES.md conjectures 'the mapping of nodesize to min_samples_split = nodesize + 1', but design.learners.forest already argues that mapping is right: randomForest marks a node with <= nodesize rows terminal. A documented difference is missing. scikit-learn's max_features documentation states that the split search 'does not stop until at least one valid partition of the node samples is found, even if it requires to effectively inspect more than max_features features'. randomForest's regTree marks the node terminal when none of the mtry sampled variables gives a split. With five binary covariates among nine and nodesize 1 for D, the sklearn trees should then grow deeper and overfit m_hat more. That matches the higher Python m_hat RMSE. I have not verified this by running anything.

findings.response: Designer: candidate_deviations.forest now leads with sklearn's split search continuing beyond max_features vs randomForest's terminal node (unverified).
findings.ruling: candidate_deviations.forest now lists the sklearn split-search behaviour first and labels it 'not verified by a run'. runs/NOTES.md item 2 lists it as a conjecture.
findings.remedy: Add the max_features search-continuation difference to candidate_deviations.forest before the gate. Optionally, on one synthetic unit only, compare the mean number of leaves of the D trees in Python and in R (randomForest treesize()) and record the result as a data-prep run.

findings.text: The port deviations are stated in synthetic dollars and compared with real-data tolerances, but the synthetic outcome is on a different scale. Synthetic Y has an out-of-fold residual RMSE of about $14,300 (rmse_l_ra_*) and t_3 noise times 8,000. net_tfa has SD $63,523, p99 $219,922 and max $1,536,798 (data/derived/sipp1991_summary.json, marginal summary only). The lasso deviation sits in the Y lasso (cor_l_min 0.994, cor_m_min 0.99999), so its effect on theta should scale with the outcome's residual noise, not with theta. runs/NOTES.md's '-$87, about 11% / 14% of the lasso tolerance' can therefore understate the real-data deviation several-fold. A crude rescaling by the SD ratio (x4.5, about -$390) would move the K = 5 lasso failure probability from about 0.01 to about 0.14. The $25 floors in the pass rules and the 'max <= $25' lasso rule have the same scale problem. The forest deviation (D side, proportional to theta) is less affected (F7).

findings.response: Designer: check_learner_ports.scale_limitation states that synthetic dollars (residual RMSE ~$14,300 vs SD $63,523) can understate the Y-side lasso shift ~4.5x and that the $25 floors are synthetic; p_outside_if_shift_x4_5 recorded for lasso cells.
findings.ruling: check_learner_ports.scale_limitation states the scale problem and that the $25 floors are synthetic. The zero-threshold correction also removed the Y-lasso shift itself (re-run: +$0.04, max $0.36, cor_l_min 0.99999997), so the x4.5 rescaling now changes nothing (p_outside_if_shift_x4_5 0.005, consistent with my arithmetic).
findings.remedy: Narrow the wording, which is cheaper than a rerun. Report each port deviation in synthetic units (for example shift / synthetic theta SE, and shift / rms_seed) and say it is on a synthetic outcome lighter-tailed and about 4.5 times smaller in scale than net_tfa. Do not present a Y-side deviation as a percentage of a real-data tolerance. Fix the NOTES '21x' (it is 13x).

findings.text: Two pieces of evidence the design relies on are not recorded. (1) runs/NOTES.md supports the lasso explanation, 'hdm's solution is unconverged', with 'an unlogged scratchpad diagnostic on one 400-row synthetic training fold' (KKT violations). That is a different training size from the check's, and there is no script, run or output. (2) The primary c = 0.5 rests on the claim that hdm 0.1.0 / 0.2.0, the versions the authors could have run, reset c to 0.5. Task s-hdm-source, which was to put that source reading in sources/, is still 'todo'. check-learner-ports shows only that the installed 0.3.2 does this. sources/notes.md line 82 still says the authors fit rlasso with 'c = 1.1'.

findings.text: The timing behind design.splits is contradicted by the only end-to-end timing of the final ports. The check's Python phase (10 units, K = 2, all five learners, the dml_plr.py functions, loky n_jobs = -1, one BLAS thread per fit) took 254 s wall. The design's timing model predicts about 425 s serial (42.5 s per unit from runs/timing-synthetic/timing.json, as design.check_learner_ports.time also says) divided by the 3.3-4.1 speed-up, i.e. 104-129 s. That is 2.0-2.4 times faster than measured. Possible reasons: the final rlasso_fit_predict drops the warm_start the prototype timed (runs/NOTES.md); the prototype timed lasso and nnet without the one-thread BLAS limit the main runs impose; other workloads were running on the machine. If the ratio carries over, the 34-43 minute estimate becomes about 70-100 minutes against the 60-minute budget. design.splits.rule forbids changing S after the runs start, so the gate is the last legitimate point to re-fix S.
findings.evidence: runs/check-learner-ports/stdout.log ('Python ports done: 200 fits, 254 s wall'); runs/timing-synthetic/timing.json; design.splits.timing_estimate; design.check_learner_ports.time; code/dml_plr.py rlasso_fit_predict vs code/timing_synthetic.py
findings.response: Designer: PI ruling (b) recorded in design.splits.rule and threats: S stays; a budget overrun (70-100 min possible) is disclosed, not traded for power.
findings.ruling: PI ruling (b) is recorded in design.splits.rule and threats[13]: S stays as fixed, and any overrun is disclosed rather than traded for power. Also, the re-run of check-learner-ports finished its Python phase in 110 s wall (runs/NOTES.md), which is inside the timing model's 104-129 s. So the 254 s first run looks like a load outlier, not a model error. The '70-100 minutes possible' wording in design.splits is now conservative rather than wrong.
findings.remedy: Before the gate, re-time dml_plr.run itself on a synthetic Y/D (one or two splits per learner, the real parallel setup) and re-fix S from that. Or have the PI accept now, in plan.json, a disclosed overrun with S unchanged.

findings.text: plan.json says that hdm 0.1.0 behaves like the primary c = 0.5. It does not, according to the workspace's own source record. design.learners.lasso.penalty_constant_note says the primary c = 0.5 is 'the behaviour of hdm 0.1.0/0.2.0'. candidate_deviations.lasso[0] says 'c = 0.5 assumed (hdm 0.1/0.2.0/0.3.x behaviour)'. But sources/hdm_penalty.md sections 3-5 show that 0.1.0 computes lambda0 with sqrt(2 log(2p log n / gamma)), which equals the qnorm formula at c of about 0.62 (0.6205 at K = 2, 0.6212 at K = 5). It also says a stale 0.1.0 install 'cannot be excluded'. The same note still says the 0.1.0/0.2.0 reading is 'unverified in the workspace' until s-hdm-source is done, but that task is done. The practical effect is small: c of about 0.62 lies between the primary 0.5 and sens-lasso-c11's 1.1, so the sensitivity run brackets it. But the paper will inherit a wrong statement about which hdm versions the primary lasso reproduces.

findings.ruling: Cheapest remedy: reword. Say the primary c = 0.5 reproduces hdm 0.2.0, 0.3.1 and 0.3.2. Say hdm 0.1.0 corresponds to an effective c of about 0.62 and 0.2.3 to 1.1, both bracketed by sens-lasso-c11. Delete the 'until then unverified' sentence. No new run is needed.

findings.text: A failed lasso cell has a fixed reading against the port shift, but no fixed reading against the penalty-constant sensitivity run. With the corrected port the measured lasso shift is +$0.04, so any lasso cell outside its tolerance will read 'not explained by the measured deviation' (runs/NOTES.md says so itself). The only remaining explanation on the candidate list is then candidate_deviations.lasso[0], c = 1.1, and sens-lasso-c11 is run 'reported next to the main lasso cells'. Nothing fixed in advance says how sens-lasso-c11 may be used to read a failed lasso cell. A post-hoc sentence such as 'the lasso cell fails at c = 0.5 but sens-lasso-c11 lies inside the tolerance, so the authors probably used c = 1.1' is open. The workspace's own evidence (sources/hdm_penalty.md section 5) says c = 1.1 is inconsistent with the dates of the published numbers. The verdict is unaffected, so this is minor.

findings.ruling: Cheapest remedy: one sentence in decision_rules. The lasso cells of sens-lasso-c11 are compared with the published cells using the same tolerances, and the result is reported descriptively. Any statement that the authors used c = 1.1 must cite the timeline in sources/hdm_penalty.md section 5 and is labelled a conjecture. sens-lasso-c11 never changes a reading or the verdict.
